title: Spraying broad-spectrum insecticides early in the season
why: It kills the natural enemies of planthoppers, so brown planthopper numbers can explode later (called resurgence).
instead: Use resistant varieties, protect natural enemies, and spray only when pest counts pass a local threshold.

title: Irrigating with salty water or without drainage
why: Salt builds up around the roots and reduces growth and yield.
instead: Test irrigation water and soil, make sure the field drains, flush with good-quality water, and choose salt-tolerant varieties.

title: Draining deep peat for planting
why: Drained peat sinks, releases large amounts of carbon, and is prone to fire.
instead: Avoid new planting on deep peat. On existing peat plantations, manage the water table carefully.

title: Clearing primary forest for new plantations
why: Oil palm plantations hold far fewer forest species than the forest they replace.
instead: Plant on land that is already degraded, and replant existing plantations rather than expanding.

title: Burning to clear land or old palms
why: Burning causes smoke and haze, releases carbon, and harms soil life.
instead: Use zero-burning: chip or stack the old palms and vegetation and let them rot.

title: Using the same herbicide (same mode of action) every season
why: Weeds that survive pass on their resistance, and resistant weeds spread through the field and beyond.
instead: Rotate herbicide modes of action, rotate crops, and add non-chemical weed control.

title: Growing soybean on the same field year after year
why: Pests and diseases that live on soybean, such as soybean cyst nematode, build up in the soil.
instead: Rotate soybean with cereals or other non-host crops.

title: Applying heavy nitrogen fertiliser to soybean
why: High soil nitrogen can reduce nodulation and nitrogen fixation, so you pay for fertiliser the crop does not need.
instead: Rely on inoculation and root nodules. Add nitrogen only when a soil test recommends it.
